text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- A total of 90,000 jobs could be created if the government would let the unemployed work in health, elderly and child care while keeping their unemployment benefits.

- Former Swedish Prime Minister Ingvar Carlsson did not, in 1988, tell the standing committee on the constitution all he knew about the secret service's illegal bugging of a member of the Kurdish organisation PKK, a book of interviews with former Swedish ambassador Carl Lidbom shows. The PKK member was bugged as the police thought he might give them clues to who killed former Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme in 1986.

- Tough wage negotiations are coming up in Sweden as unions demand real wage increases for 1998 while employers in several sectors are so pressured that they cannot compensate for higher wages by raising prices.

- Melker Schorling, the chief executive of Swedish construction company Skanska, will take over as chairman of the group when Percy Barnevik steps down to take over at investment company Investor, newspaper sources said.

- There is an increased risk of volatility on the bourse when institutional investors increase their ownership and households' decrease theirs, says Leif Vindevag, head of research at the Stockholm Stock Exchange.

Vindevag also called for Swedish groups to strive for a better balance of foreign owners, decreasing U.S. investors' stakes, partly because of the currency risk. U.S. investors could all move in the same direction at the time of large fluctuations between the crown and the dollar, hurting the bourse, he said.
- The use of lobbying to affect political decisions is increasing.

- All of Sweden's five public pension funds will probably be allowed to buy shares next year, giving the bourse a possible injection of 100 billion crowns, according to a coming proposal by the finance ministry.
The funds could together be allowed to own a maximum of 25 percent of shares in a listed company.

Currently, three of the funds -- the so called first, second and third AP fund which together manage 550 billion crowns -- are not allowed to buy shares, while the fourth and fifth AP fund have most of their 60 billion crowns invested in shares. A sixth AP fund, with more than ten billion crowns, has started this year and is mainly to invest in small and mid-sized companies.
- Some share fund companies have misleading advertisements, according to research by the newspaper and a lawyer.

- The Stockholm Stock Exchange gives a better direct return than bank accounts. A person having his or her money in a bank account in Swedbank gets an interest rate of 3.5 percent, while a person holding Swedbank shares gets a direct return of more than four percent.
